claims.claim: Cybersecurity is the protection of computer systems, networks, and data from unauthorized access, use, disclosure, disruption, modification, or destruction. CISA defines it as the art of protecting networks, devices, and data from unauthorized access or criminal use; NIST SP 800-12 Rev. 1 quotes the statutory definition of information security as the protection of information and information systems from unauthorized access, use, disclosure, disruption, modification, or destruction.

What cybersecurity protects spans devices, data, people, and organizations. CISA's definition names networks, devices, and data; NIST SP 800-12 Rev. 1 states that systems and processes must be able to protect information, financial assets, physical assets, and employees.

The stakes of failed protection include financial loss, identity theft, disrupted services, and national security. NIST SP 800-12 Rev. 1 documents organized crime groups using phishing and malicious code to commit identity theft and online fraud, extortion and ransom attacks disrupting numerous businesses at significant cost, and terrorists seeking to exploit critical infrastructure to threaten national security; CISA names stolen card information and erased files among everyday harms.

Cybersecurity work is shared: organizations employ security teams built around roles such as analysts and incident responders, and everyday users have a role as well. The NICE Framework (NIST SP 800-181 Rev. 1) is a national lexicon that organizes cybersecurity work into work roles (e.g., cyber defense analyst, cyber defense incident responder) and explicitly notes that work roles are not job titles; CISA's individual guidance states the first step in protecting yourself is to recognize the risks.

The field's core mindset combines assuming harm can happen, defense in depth, and risk-based thinking. CISA states there is no guarantee that even with the best precautions some harms will not occur, and the goal is to minimize the chances; NIST SP 800-12 Rev. 1 defines defense in depth as multi-layered countermeasures (administrative, technical, and physical) that minimize the probability of a successful attack; NIST SP 800-12 Rev. 1 also states that because information security risk cannot be completely eliminated, the objective is an optimal balance between protecting systems and using available resources.

Cybersecurity is a career field whose work is cataloged by the NICE Framework: it serves students, job seekers, and employers as a common lexicon for describing cybersecurity work, improving how talent is identified, recruited, developed, and retained, with work roles such as cyber defense analyst, cyber defense incident responder, and security architect.

No system is perfectly secure: CISA states that even with the best precautions there is no guarantee that some harms will not happen, and NIST SP 800-12 Rev. 1 states that information security risk cannot be completely eliminated, so security success is measured by reduced likelihood, faster detection, and smaller damage rather than by absolute safety.

conflictingEvidence.issue: The two primary definitions of cybersecurity differ in wording: CISA frames it as protecting networks, devices, and data from unauthorized access or criminal use, while NIST (via the statutory definition in 44 U.S.C. 3542 quoted in SP 800-12 Rev. 1) frames it as protecting information and information systems from unauthorized access, use, disclosure, disruption, modification, or destruction.
positions: CISA: 'the art of protecting networks, devices, and data from unauthorized access or criminal use'
NIST/44 U.S.C. 3542: 'the protection of information and information systems from unauthorized access, use, disclosure, disruption, modification, or destruction'
conflictingEvidence.resolution: Not a substantive conflict: both describe protection of computing resources and the information they carry against unauthorized or harmful action. The lesson presents the two framings as complementary and builds a working definition from their common core, attributing each framing to its source.

Supports: the statutory definition of information security quoted from 44 U.S.C. 3542 ('the protection of information and information systems from unauthorized access, use, disclosure, disruption, modification, or destruction'); the scope of protection including information, financial assets, physical assets, and employees; defense in depth as multi-layered administrative, technical, and physical countermeasures that minimize the probability of a successful attack; the statements that information security risk cannot be completely eliminated and that the objective is an optimal balance between protection and available resources; and stakes including identity theft and online fraud by criminal groups, extortion/ransom attacks disrupting businesses at significant cost, and terrorists threatening national security through critical infrastructure. sourceRecords.title: What is Cybersecurity? (CISA, released February 1, 2021)
sourceRecords.notes: cisa.gov blocks automated fetchers (Akamai access denied on direct curl); read an Internet Archive capture of the page (web.archive.org 2025 snapshot, 2026-08-21) whose text matched the known canonical content; the canonical cisa.gov URL is registered. Supports: the definition of cybersecurity as 'the art of protecting networks, devices, and data from unauthorized access or criminal use and the practice of ensuring confidentiality, integrity, and availability of information'; everyday harms including attackers stealing credit card information for unauthorized purchases and malware erasing systems; the honest limit that there is no guarantee even with the best precautions that some harms will not occur, with steps to minimize the chances; and the individual role ('the first step in protecting yourself is to recognize the risks'). Facts synthesized into original prose; no wording reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: NIST Special Publication 800-181 Revision 1: Workforce Framework for Cybersecurity (NICE Framework)
sourceRecords.provider: National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST)
sourceRecords.license: U.S. Government work; not subject to copyright in the United States
sourceRecords.notes: Read the PDF text layer directly (downloaded from nvlpubs.nist.gov, ~0.5 MB) on 2026-08-21. Supports: the NICE Framework as a common, consistent lexicon that categorizes and describes cybersecurity work and improves how cybersecurity talent is identified, recruited, developed, and retained; work roles as the unit of cybersecurity work, with examples including cyber defense analyst (PR-CDA-001), cyber defense incident responder (PR-CIR-001), security architect (SP-ARC-002), and security control assessor; the explicit statement that work roles are not synonymous with job titles (one role may carry many titles, several roles may combine into one job); and example cybersecurity teams built around work. Facts synthesized into original prose; no wording reproduced.
